    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making.
    • It has been revealed that the Bucks kept kicking the can down the road.
    • Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making. The Miami Heat were a rumored suitor for Antetokounmpo, who played his first 13 NBA seasons in Milwaukee, as far back as the buildup to his possible 2021 free agency, which the Bucks averted by trading for Jrue Holiday and ultimately winning a championship.

    It has been revealed that the Bucks kept kicking the can down the road. They secured another extension with Antetokounmpo in 2023 by trading for Damian Lillard. They stuck their fingers in their ears and pretended everything was fine when Lillard tore his Achilles in 2025, in the process bypassing the chance to trade Antetokounmpo with multiple years left on his contract when they could have maximized his trade value. In the end, though, Heat president Pat Riley did what he has done so many times before: he got his man.

    Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land. We have around four weeks of data on how these teams are going to look after one of the bigger blockbusters in recent NBA history, so with their first head-to-head bout at hand, let's regrade the trade based on everything we now know.

    According to recent reports, let's start with the obvious positive: despite age- and injury-related fears, Antetokounmpo is still mostly himself. He is, by both the counting stats and the all-in-ones, playing either at the level of his Milwaukee peak or somewhere relatively close. He has at the very least been a top 10 player in the NBA this season, and you could argue him into the top five. Miami paid an All-NBA price and has gotten an All-NBA player.

    Recent findings suggest that there are slight signs of slipping in his age-32 season that merit some examination, though they don't come close to triggering any real alarms. His free-throw rate is lower than it's been since 2018, for instance, but it's still near the top of the league. He's scoring 1.38 points per possession when shooting at the rim -- a very good figure that rates him in the 82nd percentile league-wide, per Synergy Sports. We just judge Antetokounmpo on a curve because he was in the 95th percentile last season and generally hovered around the mid-90s when he was winning MVPs and his 2021 championship.

    This is, again, not a significant concern. He's still great, and he's supplementing his rim finishing with significant improvement from mid-range. After shooting below 39% from mid-range over the past five seasons combined, he's above 51% so far this season. We can say pretty safely at this point that the 3-point shot is never coming for Antetokounmpo, so this shot will be his pathway to both aging gracefully and combating the walls he'll see at the rim in the playoffs. If this is sustainable, it extends his prime another year or two and makes him close to unguardable while he remains near his physical peak. Thus far, last year's calf injuries have not recurred.

    Industry observers note that he's slipped defensively. That's almost undeniable. He contested around nine shots per game when he won Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. He's down to around six this season, and opponents are shooting 6% worse within six feet of the basket against Antetokounmpo than they are otherwise, per NBA.com tracking data. That figure was 20.4% in 2020. The all-in-ones share this basic opinion: still good, no longer great. The tape indicates an older player who paces himself defensively. He can still summon greatness for stretches, but he's not in the All-Defense mix seriously anymore.

    Recent findings suggest that that brings us to the bigger picture. When you trade as much as Miami did, the question is never just whether the player is good enough to justify the cost, but whether the team is. Heat fans would point to the team's ongoing 8-2 stretch following its 0-4 start to suggest that it was. Count me as a remaining skeptic.

    According to recent reports, most of those victories came against either the bottom of the league -- the Kings, the Jazz, they needed overtime to beat the Clippers! -- or injured opponents. No Tyrese Haliburton in the Pacers win. No Jalen Duren against the Pistons. No Evan Mobley against the Cavaliers. No Amen Thompson against the Rockets, playing the second night of a back-to-back. They've faced only two true heavy hitters at full strength, the Lakers and Timberwolves, and they stood no chance against either.

    The theory of this team relies on a top-five defense. The offense is simply too reliant on shot creation out of its bigs -- Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- to be the leading unit for a champion. The early defensive returns have thus far been discouraging, though in fairness, no team has been unluckier on wide-open opponents' 3s. Even during the 8-2 stretch, they're allowing 48.4 points in the paint per game, a well-below-average figure. Their transition defense is nothing special and they're so-so rebounders. They've hung their hat on turnover-generation, but they're by no means elite on that front. The raw numbers are bad. The truth is closer to fine when you factor in luck. They haven't been great, which is what they need to be.

    Part of the problem is that they need to play defensively deficient players -- most notably Klay Thompson and, if he eventually re-earns his rotation spot, Tim Hardaway Jr. -- in order to survive offensively. You can get away with that if everyone else is great. Antetokounmpo has taken a step back. Andrew Wiggins has been a mess. Erik Spoelstra is a defensive miracle worker, but the players here just haven't lived up to expectations. Davion Mitchell has become so important offensively that even he's slipped a bit on that end.

    Mitchell's playmaking has been a godsend, and a pretty surprising one in context. The Heat tried and failed to get the Bucks to take Mitchell instead of Kasparas Jakučionis in the trade. There's no telling how bad things would be without Mitchell at this stage, but we're still talking about a pretty limited scorer who nearly doubled his 3-point volume and free throw attempt rate in a single season. Miami probably can't expect him to carry this sort of burden forever. Pelle Larsson is more of a connector than a creator in his own right. Down the line, another guard who can create off of the dribble is probably needed here, especially without a strong Antetokounmpo-Adebayo two-man game forming thus far.

    It has been revealed that the paths to improvement here are narrow here. The Heat are pressed up against a first-apron hard cap, and they'd need Charlotte's cooperation to amend the protection on their 2027 selection if they wanted to trade even a single first-round pick at this deadline. It's going to take a little while to meaningfully upgrade the supporting talent here, and the rest of the Heat offseason reflected that.

    It has been revealed that they could have perhaps generated the cap flexibility to retain Norman Powell. They elected instead to let him walk, and when they extended Wiggins, they chose to front-load the deal by using his player option rather than spreading the money out to create more immediate hard cap room. Rather than signing a mid-level free agent to a multi-year deal, they added the older Hardaway on just a one-year contract, presumably to maintain optionality going into next summer.

    Industry observers note that if Antetokounmpo were 28, this patience might make sense. He turns 32 in less than a month. The time to go all-in around him is now. It's an ironic middle ground that the Heat have put themselves in. Miami could justify the cost it paid for Antetokounmpo only through immediate contention, yet they're slow-playing the roster build in what you would expect, just based on the standard aging curve, to be the best individual season left in his career. It really doesn't make sense to do this halfway.

    We're talking about the Heat here. They've made the Finals with less talent than they have now, and they are organizationally opposed to intentional rebuilds. There was never a conversation here about, say, trading Adebayo and starting over as opposed to pushing chips in for someone like Antetokounmpo. But if a few years pass and the Heat don't at least make the conference finals with this core, it's going to be worth wondering if that's the path they should have taken. The early returns here are mixed. The Heat bet their future on a single player. He may be good enough to warrant that investment, but the jury's still out on whether their team actually is.

    Industry observers note that the Bucks dug themselves an enormous hole by refusing to trade Antetokounmpo when the whole world knew they should have. It was over the moment Lillard tore his Achilles. At that point, Antetokounmpo had two years left on his contract, so hypothetical rental trades would have been feasible. He was younger and he hadn't yet lost a year to calf injuries, so his value was higher. Asset-rich teams like the Spurs and Rockets might have been interested. Had the Bucks moved Antetokounmpo in 2025, they would have gotten substantially more than they wound up getting. Instead, they made the disastrous decision not only to keep him but also to waive and stretch Lillard to sign Myles Turner. Yikes.

    In a recent development, when the Bucks finally realized they'd reached the point of no return, Antetokounmpo, as an expiring contract, had complete control of the situation. At least four teams with strong offers were turned away because Antetokounmpo simply wasn't interested in extending with them, according to ESPN. He only wanted the Heat or Celtics. Given those circumstances, the Bucks still managed the negotiations as well as they reasonably could have. They used the Celtics as an effective scare tactic to compel Miami to give up pretty much all of its available draft capital, plus Jakučionis instead of Mitchell.

    You can win a negotiation and still lose a trade, though, when most of the things the other team had to give in a trade just weren't that valuable. The big swing piece here was Kel'El Ware, an extremely high-risk, high-reward young big man with star-level raw talent and a pretty iffy reputation when it comes to his motor and commitment. The Bucks, thus far, have gotten the worst version of him. He's playing less in his third season with the Bucks than he did in two years with the Heat despite being on the worst roster of his career. He's missing shots everywhere, his defense has been miserable, and if he's ever going to reach that sky-high ceiling, it's probably going to have to come on his third team.

    Industry observers note that that, in a nutshell, is the problem here. The Bucks traded the greatest player in franchise history, one of the 25 or so best players the league has ever seen, and got no one who could credibly be considered a cornerstone moving forward. Ware looks like a swing and a miss. It's too early to say much on Nate Ament, but he's a No. 13 overall draft pick, so odds are, he's going to be fine and not much better. Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. are both about what they expected, but both will need to be paid next summer. Herro's presence exacerbates a preexisting glut of guards. His presence has forced last year's breakout guard, Ryan Rollins, to the bench. Maybe that makes him a bit cheaper as a free agent next summer. It also probably sours him on a future in Milwaukee.

    Speaking of the guard glut, the Gary Trent Jr. investigation looms large over this trade. The NBA set a notable precedent in the Kawhi Leonard case that it is willing to strip teams of draft picks acquired through trade. This is notable because the Bucks have so little control over their own first-round picks moving forward. The picks they got from the Heat in 2031 and 2033, at least for now, are the crown jewels of this trade. Both of them are theoretically vulnerable if the NBA finds that the Bucks circumvented the salary cap.

    It's even worth wondering if the Bucks should or could have used the Antetokounmpo situation as an escape hatch on any preexisting agreements with Trent, if one actually existed. If the Bucks felt an obligation to pay Trent more than the market suggested he was worth, and if they knew they had so many guards that he was unlikely to factor into their rotation (he played less than 40 total minutes before bizarrely leading the Bucks in playing time in Sunday's loss to the Hawks despite coming off the bench), then why not use the leverage Antetokounmpo's availability granted them to foist Trent on Miami through a sign-and-trade? Of course, if the Bucks had the foresight to do this, they probably wouldn't be in this situation in the first place. For now, the investigation is ongoing and we know little beyond the sheer ridiculousness of the contract itself.

    Sources indicate that the Bucks are 1-13 as of this writing. That, roughly, was to be expected. This was a bad team with Antetokounmpo, so inevitably, removing an MVP candidate was going to make it far worse. But to leave a trade involving a player of that caliber without a single blue-chip player or draft pick is frankly embarrassing.

    The Bucks bungled this Antetokounmpo saga for a year, and even if they managed its end stages properly, they'd dug themselves so deep a hole that there was just no obvious way out of it. Now, it seems they may well have made the situation worse with Trent after the fact. This was an organization-wide debacle.

    The Timing Game – MH

    📅 31 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 31.03.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 1 Kommentar.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Timing Game describes a playing philosophy in which the right moment of an action is crucial.
    • “Brighton is a master of passing the ball to the free man but recognising when to pass the ball to the free man and moving at the right time.” – Pep Guardiola.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 31.03.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 1 Kommentar.

    Recent findings suggest that the Timing Game describes a playing philosophy in which the right moment of an action is crucial. It not only allows pressing traps to be reversed but also enables teams to break down deep defensive blocks with precision. In the Premier League, Brighton’s then-manager Roberto De Zerbi took this tactical approach to a fresh level.

    “Brighton is a master of passing the ball to the free man but recognising when to pass the ball to the free man and moving at the right time.” – Pep Guardiola.

    The core idea of the Timing Game is to react to the opponent’s movement at precisely the right moment. Pressing traps can be reversed by first triggering and manipulating the opponent’s press and then bypassing it through changes in speed and direction. Since opposition pressing actions are highly dynamic, this approach is particularly effective against high-pressing teams. Consequently, the Timing Game allows teams to dominate pressing situations in their own buildup play. Additionally, because opponent movements can be triggered independently of the game phase, the Timing Game can also be applied against deep defensive blocks.

    Regarding the role of timing in De Zerbi’s buildup play, René Maric (RM) explained in a 2023 interview with SkySports:.

    „The biggest thing in the build-up is the control of rhythm. If you look at Guardiola, he does it with the speed of the passes and then they carry the ball when they don’t have pressure. De Zerbi does it more with the moment of the pass, the lure, the sole on the ball, opening space with the pass rather than the carry. How you control the rhythm and progress through space will be substantial in the future. That development has already started.“.

    Sources indicate that this article examines the dimensions and functioning of the Timing Game. Additionally, it analyzes the impact of a team’s own positioning, as well as the manipulation, anticipation, and triggering of the opponent’s press (or movements). The following sections will then explore the action of bypassing the opponent, the potential problems that arise within the Timing Game, and possible solutions to these challenges.

    This section is an attempt to highlight the various facets of the Timing Game and football in general. Different playing philosophies prioritize different dimensions. In the Timing Game described here, particular focus is placed on the timing of dynamics in relation to the opponent.

    Recent findings suggest that to gain a better understanding of the principles of the Timing Game, the following section presents and explains its different dimensions. This makes it clear how the Timing Game differs from the focus of positional play and relationism but can also be combined with them. Although the game dimensions are less vital for the practical implementation of the Timing Game, they can be useful for further developing this concept or other coaching philosophies.

    The most key dimension of the Timing Game is the temporal dimension. The crucial factors are the speed and timing of decision-making. The timing of a progressive action should generally coincide with the opponent’s movement. The primary focus is therefore on the exact moment of an action.

    Recent findings suggest that A second notable dimension is that of dynamics. The dynamic dimension of the Timing Game revolves around explosiveness and changes in rhythm. Changes in dynamics can be decisive both in relation to one’s own play and in terms of directional shifts in relation to the opponent. Ultimately, the goal is to create the strongest possible reciprocal acceleration in the opponent.

    Industry observers note that in the dimension of individual performance factors, the focus is on footballing competencies such as technical and athletic abilities. In the Timing Game, ball control is a crucial factor, as it significantly affects a player’s pressing resistance. Ball control involves both the ability to recognize a situation and the technical capability to handle the ball under pressure at any time. This skill is particularly crucial in the Timing Game, as it provides an advantage during the opponent’s pressing phase.

    According to recent reports, the causal-relational dimension deals with the cause-and-effect principle in interactions between teammates and opponents. There is a causal relationship both between the opponent’s defensive approach and the method of bypassing them, as well as between a teammate’s action and the resulting ball action. The following examples illustrate this:.

    In relationism, interactions between teammates are particularly emphasized to enable optimal interplay. Due to the complexity of this dimension, I have linked MR’s seminar “The Future of the Game” here.

    Recent findings suggest that in the spatial dimension, the focus is on controlling specific zones of the pitch. This is particularly crucial in positional play, where the aim is to control the game through ball possession and spatial occupation. In the Timing Game, however, the goal is to reach the space behind the opponent. Since this space is constantly changing, it cannot strictly be defined as a fixed pitch zone. However, the spatial dimension does play a role in the preparatory positioning of the Timing Game. This article contains a dedicated section on the optimal positioning in preparation for the Timing Game.

    Recent findings suggest that in the Timing Game, the moment of an action is primarily decisive. The moment of action is always triggered by the opponent’s movement. The more intense the opponent’s movement, the easier it is to bypass them. This is because, once the Timing Game is triggered, the opponent should be bypassed as diagonally opposed to their movement as possible. This forces the opponent into a maximal change of direction and dynamics.

    The pressing near one’s own penalty area is bypassed diagonally opposite to the direction of the press.

    Sources indicate that A temporal advantage is created over the opponent, who initially has to accelerate in the opposite direction and loses time. The space that opens up behind the advancing opponent can be played most effectively. Representing the functioning of the Timing Game, the principle of “Lure and Shock” could be used. The opponent is first “lured” into the movement and then “shocked” by being bypassed.

    The Timing Game is particularly effective during the opponent’s transition from a deeper to a higher pressing setup. At the moment of transition between ordered pressing phases, the opponent’s structure is often lacking, as the distances between the players change. Additionally, movement is present on all positions of the opponent, which can be exploited for the Timing Game. The direction of the opponent’s movement is also crucial, as during the transition from a deeper to a higher pressing phase, vertical movement away from the goal dominates, allowing spaces towards the opponent’s goal to be exploited.

    This specific moment of the opponent’s pressing transition into a higher setup cannot be found in the classic phase model of the game according to Van Gaal. Depending on the perspective, it would be classified as part of either the team’s own possession phase or the opponent’s possession phase, even though it is significantly more complex and interesting than other possession situations. The opponent is essentially in a type of defensive transition into attack from the opponent’s ball possession, while the own team takes advantage of this moment and transitions from their own ball possession into a kind of offensive transition.

    The Timing Game, however, does not only work during transitions between different pressing setups, but also independently of the game phase, and thus also within the framework of the opponent’s attacking press. The opponent’s movement in attacking pressing usually does not need to be triggered additionally. Instead, it is more about anticipating the moment when the opponent’s attacking press is triggered. At the moment of pressing initiation, there is a very high dynamic on multiple positions of the opponent in (diagonal) vertical directions, which allows the pressing to be bypassed with suitable movements at the moment of initiation. Particularly, the opponent’s pressing traps can be bypassed at the moment of initiation through a corresponding pre-rehearsed anticipation and movement.

    It has been revealed that depending on the individual pressing patterns of the opponent, preparations should be made for the timing and manner of bypassing. For example, man-marking in attacking pressing can be bypassed differently than ball-oriented or hybrid marking schemes. Particularly against man-marking, it is important in the Timing Game to initially provoke dynamics in the opponent through various runs, in order to then bypass them in the opposite direction. If dynamics are not created through own runs, there is often little movement from the opponent in the second and third layers that could be exploited.

    Because dynamics are also created in the opponent’s man-marking in the second and third layers, multiple layers can be bypassed.

    The pressing triggers and pressing traps also differ depending on the type of attacking press, so anticipating the moments of the Timing Game requires prior analysis of the opponent. A very commonly used pressing trigger is a backward pass to the goalkeeper from a higher defensive line. A common reaction is for the goalkeeper to play the ball long under pressure, usually resulting in a loss of possession. In the Timing Game, a team would create passing options behind the opponent through collective movements at the moment the opponent triggers their press. Specific movements and methods for bypassing the press will be discussed in more detail later in the article.

    Individual pressing patterns also include the opponent’s pressing structure itself. Here too, individual weaknesses can be diagnosed and exploited in advance. When the opponent presses from a 4-4-2, they often have an under-populated central area. Of course, this cannot be generalized, as, for example, the ball-far midfielder or an aggressive center-back may situationally reinforce the center. However, if this is not the case, an inverse run by the full-back at the moment the press is triggered could be useful to play into the space behind the press against the dynamics. It can be stated that the Timing Game, against different opponents with different individual pressing patterns, influences the movements made to bypass the press.

    The Timing Game can also work against deep-lying opponents. However, it is more difficult here because, in general, there is less movement away from the goal, and the opponent attacks in a more passive manner. The deep-lying opponent’s goal is to close the space near the goal. It will be crucial to trigger the opponent’s movement or pressing and lure the opponent out. We will go into more detail on such trigger actions later.

    In a recent development, in summary, the following rules for the Timing Game depending on the opponent’s pressing can be established: The deeper the opponent is positioned, the less dynamic movement there is away from their own goal. Therefore, the time window for bypassing the press is shorter. The more passive the opponent acts, the less frequently there is opponent movement. As a result, there will be fewer opportunities to bypass the press. Nevertheless, the Timing Game can be used independently of the game phase through trigger actions.

    The team’s formation in possession should be adapted to the challenges of the Timing Game. It should create central connections through a vertical/diagonal alignment. This way, more layers can be incorporated into the dynamics, and more passing options can be created. More passing windows open up at the moment of triggering through a variety of passing angles. In the event of a loss of possession, it also allows for more effective counter-pressing.

    It has been revealed that additionally, it can be useful to work with asymmetries and overloads. Overloading the own buildup zone is particularly effective when the opponent closes down and applies high pressure. This lures the opponent and allows them to be bypassed with a few passes. In the linked video example, De Zerbi’s Shakhtar Donetsk uses a strategy of having 7 players in their own penalty area during a goal kick to lure the opponent out.

    Nothing to see here, just a completely normal build-up pic.twitter.com/vOcvRPVKdf.

    — Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) April 28, 2022.

    Problems in the Timing Game arise when there is an overload in the own buildup zone if the opponent does not press. The progression in the game is lacking because offensive passing options are not available. Also problematic is the static overload of the last line. If players remain in their specific spaces in the last line, passing options necessary to bypass the opponent’s press are missing.

    Industry observers note that another way to structure the team to prepare for the Timing Game is by leaving a specific area vacant. If the opponent attempts to press, this space is usually left unoccupied by the opponent as well. Subsequently, the space can be attacked and played into from the second line in the opposite direction. If the space is still occupied, the numerical advantage in a ball-near area can be exploited. Real Madrid often employs such structures or space-drawing runs in preparation for their actual attacking play with the ball.

    Industry observers note that in the Timing Game, the moment the opponent begins to press must be anticipated as early as possible. Possible indicators for early recognition of a pressing moment include: the opponent’s approach towards the ball-carrying teammate, the shrinking of distances between the ball-near opponents and their teammates, and the forward dynamics of the opponent. A defensive line with equal numbers or an advancing defender is also an early recognition feature. Lastly, specific pressing triggers should be identified through video analysis in advance.

    According to recent reports, an exemplary player for effective pressing resistance is Sergio Busquets, who, with his excellent ball control, was regularly able to anticipate and resolve pressing situations. In this 2017 article, TR and MR wrote about Busquets’ qualities.

    According to recent reports, what is particularly interesting is triggering the opponent’s attacking press. There are a variety of very interesting trigger actions. One variation used by De Zerbi is the use of the sole on the ball to wait. This plays on the impatience of the opponent. The following quote and video clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of this trigger action.

    Sources indicate that “It’s so fascinating to watch (…) when the ball goes to the center back, they freeze the game. (…) As soon as the pressing action happened, they then had this meticulously designed mechanism of up-back-throughs and third man connections (…).” – Jamie Hamilton, 3rd Circle Podcast.

    — Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) January 13, 2025.

    Sources indicate that another option is a pass triggered by speed. This pass should be played as slowly as possible and as quickly as necessary. The slow pass provokes the opponent’s pressing. At the same time, by the receiver moving towards the ball, the dynamics can immediately be reversed. This facilitates the transition into the action of bypassing or dribbling past the opponent. The pass direction should ideally be diagonal toward one’s own goal. This maximizes the reversal of dynamics.

    Another approach is to play into the pressure, only to then “bounce” back into the direction of the opponent’s pressing path. The opponent is initially led to believe they have access by playing into the pressure. By bouncing the ball into the pressing direction, the opponent is forced to continue their run.

    The classic way of forcing a passive opponent into movement is dribbling. The opponent is eventually made to press. However, it is also much harder to generate a dynamic shift and surprise effect, as the dribbling is already in the direction of play. Therefore, it is helpful if dribbling-skilled players attack the opponent in order to maintain the unpredictability of the next action with quick changes of direction. Alternatively, passes that bypass the opponent after dribbling in the opposite direction of the dribble path can create a dynamic shift in the opponent.

    Against deep-lying opponents, the inside diagonal is a good method to force defenders on the last line to step out a few meters. When the ball is played diagonally from the outside to the center, the central defender steps out a few steps. This can be exploited in the opposite direction. The effect is enhanced by a player letting the ball pass, as immediately after, the defender’s back can be attacked. This move is known in relationism as Escadinha.

    — Svids (@Svids8) February 23, 2025.

    After the pressing trigger, the opponent should be bypassed through dynamic, diagonal directional changes. The direction of the first action should ideally not move away from the pressure but rather target, go over, or through it to attack the opponent’s movement. Instead of directly passing to the free player (e.g., the goalkeeper), a progressive, diagonal ball should be chosen.

    Recent findings suggest that to create passing options in the desired direction, specific movements are crucial. There are also various fundamental principles for this. The start of the ball action should be as late as possible but as early as necessary.

    The timing of the movement of teammates should coincide with the moment the press begins, so they can be available to receive the ball under pressure, but not too early to avoid being caught by the opponent’s dynamic.

    Dynamic movement should also be generated in the second and third layers to have the opportunity to bypass multiple layers. Otherwise, there is a risk of opponents from the second layer, who create covering shadows, not being affected by the opposing dynamic. In a less compact space behind the first pressing line, the dynamics can occur in stages, so the layers are played one after the other.

    It is important that after an action, the next layer should be attacked immediately to maintain the dynamic.

    The decisive action to overcome the opponent can be individual, group, or team tactical in nature. Below are specific examples of such actions.

    In a recent development, A feint in the moment of pressing initiation can lead to bypassing the opponent. In the linked video, Musiala’s movement at the right moment leads to the goal. Although this movement is likely executed intuitively by Musiala at the right time, it can certainly be tactically repeated. The feint falls into the above-described phase of the pressing transition from a deeper to a higher pressing line, which is why Denmark’s player spacing is incorrect and the deep coverage is absent.

    Industry observers note that brilliant angle of Jamal Musiala’s goal from last night. 🇩🇪#Germany #Denmark #Euro #Analysis pic.twitter.com/xl2MDgvXwb.

    — Jamie Kyte (@jamielkyte) June 30, 2024.

    Individually tactical, the first touch can be used both as a triggering action and as an overcoming action. By skillfully triggering the opponent’s movement, it may be enough to simply play the ball past the opponent or through their legs. The first touch is made as far as possible but as close as necessary to allow the player to regain possession of the ball immediately in front of the opponent. This is clearly seen at the very beginning of Woltemade’s first goal in the following video.

    ⚽#woltemade #u21 pic.twitter.com/mpdKiB4inJ.

    — ran (@ransport) March 25, 2025.

    The no-look pass can also be a variant to surprise the opponent against the dynamics and running direction.

    Madrid pic.twitter.com/z2nyPVIuPi.

    — Svids (@Svids8) December 19, 2024.

    According to recent reports, florian Wirtz’s dribbles may initially seem unremarkable. However, upon closer observation, it becomes clear that Wirtz uses slight delays instead of flashy tricks to trigger the opponent’s movement, and then he moves the ball past the defender. This is also a form of timing play at the individual tactical level.

    @MunichComps pic.twitter.com/qNsq4Ljltc.

    — thomassist (@thomassist25_) January 27, 2025.

    Sources indicate that on the group tactical level, up-back-through (steil-klatsch) combinations are ideal for breaking into depth at the right moment. Here, the previously described positioning in preparation for the timing play is crucial. As many levels as possible should be occupied to open passing angles and options. The lay-off play has the advantage of being able to overcome the opponent with simple passes. It is remarkable how each of these passes is played against the opponent’s pressing direction, preventing the opponent from getting access to the ball.

    — ファンキーヤング (@funkyyoung) November 19, 2024.

    Different variations of the play through the third man are also very effective. In the following video, the effectiveness can be admired at minute 0:13, using the example of the left center-back starting in the wrong direction.

    — Svids (@Svids8) February 20, 2025.

    Other possibilities in the group tactical area include one-twos against the dynamics, space-creating runs, counter movements, or dynamic zone rotations.

    According to recent reports, there are also team tactical variations for overcoming the opponent in the timing game. One such variation is playing the second ball directly into the backline with an appropriate zone overload at the moment the pressing is triggered. The preparatory positioning is the team tactical element here.

    It has been revealed that A team tactical counter movement could also be considered, where all players in the forward zones drop back, increasing the pressing distance to create more dynamic movement. At the same time, a player from the second line attacks deeply in the opposite direction.

    One problem with the timing play is overcoming the covering shadow of the first pressing opponent. As the approaching opponent generates an increasingly larger covering shadow in a well-prepared pressing situation, passing options become limited. This can be solved through an individual tactical overcoming action, such as a dribble, a first touch, or others. Additionally, certain combination plays can help overcome the first pressing player. A back-up-back-through combination could be effective, where the first pass is played over a short distance to a nearby teammate (back), followed by an up-back-through combination to open fresh passing angles.

    The short back pass to the goalkeeper, who has moved up into the defensive line, can bypass the covering shadow of the first pressing player.

    Another problem could arise against teams with a very high pressing intensity. Since it is necessary to play into the pressure and trigger the pressing, one is systematically exposed to this high intensity repeatedly. However, this can also be used to one’s advantage. Opponents with high intensity also have high dynamics, which can be played against with greater effectiveness. Additionally, there is usually a high number of opponents in the attacking zones. Therefore, it is advisable to attack the farthest free space as directly as possible.

    Recent findings suggest that hybrid pressing can also cause problems in the timings game. Since individual players act in specific spaces, responding situationally to regain possession of the ball, they do not necessarily carry the dynamics of the pressing players. As a result, they are more difficult to play past. However, certain off-ball runs could provide solutions here. One example would be the outside defender making a diagonal run into space far from the ball.

    Lastly, there are issues when pressing the opponent during goal kicks. All playing philosophies face problems here, as the conditions to break out of the situation are not ideal. The ball is not in motion, the opponent can organize, and the playing field is limited by the goal line behind. Additionally, the risk is higher due to the proximity to the goal. The timings game would generate dynamics in the opponent by various runs from teammates, in order to reach the opponent’s back at the right moment.

    Sources indicate that the concept of dynamically timing a play to exploit the opponent’s movement at the right moment is already seen in practice. However, with a more deliberate approach, it can become more accessible to a wider range of players and even more effective. It holds the potential to bypass pressing traps and break down deep-lying defenses. It is not only applicable throughout the field but can also be effective with different numbers of players.

    The dynamic timing play concept developed here is heavily focused on the reference point of the “opponent.” Another possible concept of timing could place more emphasis on the teammate, focusing on relational interactions between players. This concept would be more closely aligned with the relationalism theory. Using the dimensions outlined here, different game concepts can be created and further developed.

    Recent findings suggest that the timing play should be used as a complementary element to complete one’s overall playing philosophy. It provides a different perspective on tactical analysis than what would be possible with static graphics, such as those on a tactic board. Therefore, it should expand an analyst’s perspective on this complex game by adding an additional dimension.

    Which team needs Tarik Skubal the most? Ranking the suitors for the best free agent available

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that as we emerge from the recent General Manager Meetings and move toward the expected Dec.
    • It has been revealed that the decorated lefty, who soon turns 30, is our No.
    • In a recent development, "Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that as we emerge from the recent General Manager Meetings and move toward the expected Dec. 1 lockout of the players by MLB owners, we might see an accelerated pace of activity soon. The most tantalizing possibility is that ace and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the undisputed top talent on the free agent market this winter, will sign before the sport shuts down for an indeterminate amount of time.

    It has been revealed that the decorated lefty, who soon turns 30, is our No. 1 free agent of the 2026-27 class, and it's not an especially close call. Here's part of our write-up:.

    In a recent development, "Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He highlighted few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself.".

    Will he set the record for the biggest contract ever signed by a pitcher? Will Skubal fetch the highest average annual salary for a pitcher? Will he top $400 million? Those are all reasonable questions to ask. First, though, there's a question to be asked about the teams that are already pursuing him the most vigorously. That question is, which team needs him the most? We're restricting our discussion to the five teams that have been most reliably linked to Skubal so far this offseason. We're already hearing reports of surprise teams, and it's always possible a surprise late bidder will enter the fray and even win his signature, but for now, these five clubs are the favorites. This, then, is an ordering of those teams based on which desperately needs a talent like Skubal in order to reach their goals in 2027 and beyond. Let's get to it, in order from "needs him the most" to "needs him but not as urgently as the teams ahead of them" ….

    In a recent development, the Cubs are in contention mode and in need of roster improvements if they're going to run down the world champion Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Central. The rotation is without question the most pressing need for Chicago. Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, David Peterson, and deadline acquisition Clay Holmes are all free agents. Justin Steele hasn't taken the mound at the big-league level since early in the 2025 season thanks to UCL surgery and a halting recovery process. While he's expected to be ready for 2027, he's not exactly a known quantity right now. Young upsider Cade Horton may not be back until midseason after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and Ben Brown, who recently had neck surgery, may be on a similar timeline. So, yes, the Cubs need a lot of rotation help, and Skubal would give them the true frontline ace they'd lack even if everyone were healthy. Unfortunately for the Cubs fans, it sounds like the Ricketts aren't willing to be truly competitive for his services.

    Coming off the grave disappointments of 2026, the Mets could certainly use a headline-grabbing addition to improve their chances in 2027 and inspire a surely disaffected fan base. Beyond that, the Mets need more starting pitching to accompany promising young Nolan McLean. Christian Scott seems like a lock, but he doesn't project as a frontliner. They have some depth options for the back end, but they need a true needle-mover like Skubal at the very front. That's especially the case in what figures to be a hotly competitive NL East in 2027. Thus far, David Stearns and owner Steve Cohen sound committed to making a good-faith run at Skubal.

    The Padres have a lot of work to do if they're going to earn a fourth straight playoff appearance. Speaking of which, the rotation is crying out for help right about now. They lost Dylan Cease to free agency last winter, and this time Michael King may be bound elsewhere, too. The Pads declined their club option on Nick Pivetta, and while they hope to bring him back on more favorable terms, there's no guarantee they'll be able to do that. Yes, Joe Musgrove will be back, but how much can he give them and how effective will he be? They'll need even more help if Adrian Morejon, a lockdown bulk reliever and possible starter-conversion project, signs elsewhere. Skubal's made to order, and signing the top talent on the market would be a strong signal by new owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones that the team's recent tradition of spending and contending won't be fading away.

    It has been revealed that the Dodgers self-evidently needed Skubal enough to acquire him from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the deadline and do so at significant cost. On paper, the Dodgers aren't as desperate for rotation help as the teams ahead of them on this list, but there's still a need. Yoshinobu Yamamoto is a certifiable ace, but behind him Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are established health and durability risks. Shohei Ohtani is something of an unknown, at least insofar as his pitching is concerned right now, and thus far Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan have not proved worthy of being relied upon. One can squint and see the Dodgers' current championship window closing in the reasonably near future, which means that's all the more reason to push the chips in now. Retaining the elite services of Skubal would greatly aid the cause in 2027.

    In a recent development, eyeball a rotation that already includes Dylan Cease, José Soriano, and Trey Yesavage, and you might think it doesn't need much more. And maybe it doesn't. As a matter of principle, though, any team with contending aspirations should be interested in a top-shelf ace when he hits the market. The Jays, who in recent years have invested in the roster at commendable levels, are no doubt dreaming of a Skubal-Cease one-two punch that would be the envy of, oh, every other team in baseball. There's also depth to think about. In particular, Cody Ponce is a bit of an unknown coming off knee surgery that ended his 2026 season in the middle of his first start. Addressing the offense probably should be more of a priority for the Jays this winter, but, again, it's Tarik Skubal, and the likes of Tarik Skubal make any team better.
